source.title: SAE regularization produces more interpretable models

record.file_problem: None; the full post text is present. The charts are referenced but their plotted values are not included in the text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether SAE training changes reconstruction error, using SAE regularization during language-model training rather than measuring the original claim’s error predictability or token-wise scaling.
record.gate_note: The post reports SAE reconstruction-quality comparisons and an end-to-end reconstruction evaluation. The chart values are not present in the text, so the rows record only the authors’ textual descriptions. The separate result that regularized models have slightly lower cross-entropy loss is not included as a row because it measures model loss, not SAE error.
record.test_reason: The study changes how the language model is trained, adding SAE losses as a regularizer. It then shows that freshly trained SAEs on the resulting weights reach a lower CE-loss increase at a given L0. None of the six versions is tested. V6 concerns whether dark matter comes from SAE-side training choices and shrinks with better SAE architectures or SAE end-to-end training. Here the SAE recipe is held fixed and the model's representation is altered, so the result says nothing about SAE-training artifacts. If anything, it shows reconstruction error depends on the model's representation. The post also never decomposes the error into linear or nonlinear parts, never compares against random errors, and never studies scaling. Its measure is overall reconstruction quality (CE-loss increase), not dark matter as the versions define it.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SAE regularization during model training yields features with lower reconstruction error at a given sparsity, apparently without hurting model loss (regularized models reach slightly lower CE loss). They say it can shape internal representations, but it is computationally demanding and shown only on a small, overfitting toy model; generalization is unknown.
record.recipe_differences: The study jointly trains SAE layers and model weights using SAE losses as regularization, then evaluates newly trained SAEs on the resulting weights. It does not test linear predictability of SAE error, per-token error scaling, or shared failure contexts across SAE sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: Results are less dependable on layer 3. The authors chose regularization coefficients to amplify the effect and did not study smaller coefficients; they note coefficients that are too large affect model performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Training a 4-layer character-level GPT-2 (Shakespeare) with SAE reconstruction and sparsity losses as a regularizer lowers the CE-loss increase of freshly trained SAEs at fixed L0 on most layers. Gains are less reliable on layer 3. End-to-end patching of reconstructions at all layers also gives a lower compound CE-loss increase.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE reconstruction error depends partly on the model's representation and can be reduced by shaping the model during training, with no loss in model performance.

record.problems: The evaluation uses a small character-based model trained on a limited Shakespeare corpus that the authors say easily overfits. Training parameters were not optimized, the coefficients were chosen to amplify the effect, and the post does not report numerical chart values or uncertainty estimates in the text. Generalization to larger models and datasets is unknown.
record.rows_left_out: None. The stated slightly lower cross-entropy loss of the regularized models was not extracted as a row because it is a model-performance measure rather than an SAE-error result.

untested.parts: Linear predictability of the SAE error from the input activation.
Per-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, shared failure contexts, and persistence of error with scale.
Whether SAE reconstruction error harms loss more than random errors of equal norm.
Whether the linear and nonlinear error components differ in learnability.
Whether circuits or steering lose behaviour without the error term.
Effect of the SAE sparsity penalty, shrinkage, dead latents, SAE objective or architecture, or SAE end-to-end training on dark matter. The SAE recipe is held fixed; only model training changes.

record.verdict_notes: No numerical values appear in the text; all results are figure-only descriptions. There are no uncertainty estimates, and the coefficients were chosen to amplify the effect. The reader's V6 'supports' label is wrong in direction of relevance. Reducing error by changing the model, with the SAE fixed, does not show dark matter is an SAE-training artifact; if anything it points toward model-side structure.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a large share of SAE error is a linear function of the input activation.
Per-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, overlap in contexts where different-sized SAEs fail, and whether error persists with scale.
Whether SAE reconstruction harms model loss more than random errors of the same size.
Whether predictable and nonlinear error components differ in their relationship to learned features or further dictionary learning.
Whether SAE-based circuits or steering lose behavior when the error term is omitted.

The study tests SAE regularization’s effect on reconstruction quality, but does not isolate sparsity penalty, shrinkage, dead latents, or objective as causes; compare architectures or end-to-end alternatives; or establish that dark matter mostly reflects SAE training.
